content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
55	
56	## Requirements
57	
58	- Python 3.11 or newer
59	- no third-party runtime dependencies
60	
61	## Run the service
62	
63	```bash
64	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
65	```
66	
67	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
68	has bound the port.
69	
70	## HTTP API
71	
72	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
73	
74	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
75	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
76	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
77	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
78	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
79	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
80	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
81	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
82	
83	### Tenants and quotas
84	
85	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
86	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
87	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
88	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
89	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
90	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
91	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
92	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
93	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
94	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
95	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
96	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
97	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
98	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
99	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
100	
101	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
102	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
103	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, queue pulls, acknowledgements,
104	and all history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics
105	queries. An empty
106	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
107	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
108	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
109	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
110	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
111	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
112	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
113	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
114	the usual `409 conflict`.
115	
116	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
117	hold:
118	
119	```http
120	PUT /quotas
121	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
122	X-Tenant-Id: acme
123	
124	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
125	```
126	
127	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
128	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
129	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
130	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
131	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
132	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
133	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
134	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
135	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
136	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
137	
138	```http
139	GET /quotas
140	X-Tenant-Id: acme
141	```
142	
143	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
144	when the tenant has declared none.
145	
146	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
147	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
148	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
149	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
150	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
151	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
152	
153	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
154	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
155	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
156	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
157	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
158	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
159	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
160	
161	### Usage metering and billing
162	
163	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
164	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
165	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
166	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
167	metered action types are:
168	
169	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
170	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
171	  definition;
172	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
173	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
174	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
175	  `schedule_triggered`;
176	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
177	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
178	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
179	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
180	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
181	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
182	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
183	  meters nothing.
184	
185	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
186	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
187	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
188	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
189	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
190	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
191	
192	```http
193	GET /usage
194	X-Tenant-Id: acme
195	```
196	
197	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
198	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
199	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
200	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
201	
202	```http
203	GET /bill
204	X-Tenant-Id: acme
205	```
206	
207	Returns the per-type bill:
208	
209	```json
210	{"bill":{"items":[
211	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
212	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
213	],"total":2100}}
214	```
215	
216	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
217	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
218	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
219	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
220	
221	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
222	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
223	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
224	
225	### Operational metrics
226	
227	```http
228	GET /metrics
229	X-Tenant-Id: acme
230	```
231	
232	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
233	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
234	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
235	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
236	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
237	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
238	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
239	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
240	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
241	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
242	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
243	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
244	
245	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
246	timestamp ending in `Z`:
247	
248	```http
249	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
250	X-Tenant-Id: acme
251	```
252	
253	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
254	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
255	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
256	  counts every recorded fact;
257	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
258	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
259	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
260	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
261	  result.
262	
263	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
264	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
265	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
266	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
267	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
268	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
269	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
270	completion or termination event.
271	
272	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
273	
274	```http
275	GET /metrics/export
276	X-Tenant-Id: acme
277	```
278	
279	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
280	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
281	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
282	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
283	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
284	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
285	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
286	
287	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
288	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
289	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
290	ordered by ascending label value:
291	
292	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
293	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
294	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
295	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
296	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
297	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
298	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
299	  unlabeled scalar samples.
300	
301	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
302	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
303	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
304	ends with a single newline.
305	
306	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
307	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
308	failures, and schedule triggers:
309	
310	```json
311	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
312	```
313	
314	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
315	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
316	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
317	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
318	  ended for that reason.
319	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
320	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
321	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
322	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
323	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
324	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
325	  another attempt, per node identifier.
326	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
327	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
328	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
329	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
330	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
331	
332	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
333	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
334	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
335	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
336	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
337	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
338	
339	### Health
340	
341	```http
342	GET /health
343	```
344	
345	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
346	
347	### Create a workflow
348	
349	```http
350	POST /workflows
351	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
352	
353	{
354	  "id": "order-flow",
355	  "nodes": [
356	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
357	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
358	  ]
359	}
360	```
361	
362	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
363	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
364	
365	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
366	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
367	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
368	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
369	
370	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
371	
372	```json
373	{
374	  "id": "order-flow",
375	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
376	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
377	}
378	```
379	
380	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
381	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
382	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
383	
384	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
385	
386	```json
387	{
388	  "id": "nightly-orders",
389	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
390	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
391	}
392	```
393	
394	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
395	
396	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
397	
398	```json
399	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
400	```
401	
402	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
403	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
404	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
405	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
406	`false`.
407	
408	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
409	
410	```json
411	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
412	```
413	
414	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
415	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
416	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
417	dependencies of its successors.
418	
419	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
420	
421	```json
422	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
423	```
424	
425	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
426	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
427	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
428	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
429	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
430	`retries_exhausted`.
431	
432	A task may instead declare an approval point:
433	
434	```json
435	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
436	```
437	
438	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
439	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
440	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
441	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
442	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
443	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
444	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
445	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
446	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
447	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
448	move the task.
449	
450	### Submit an approval decision
451	
452	```http
453	POST /executions/run-1/decision
454	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
455	
456	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
457	```
458	
459	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
460	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
461	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
462	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
463	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
464	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
465	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
466	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
467	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
468	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
469	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
470	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
471	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
472	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
473	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
474	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
475	404.
476	
477	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
478	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
479	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
480	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
481	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
482	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
483	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
484	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
485	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
486	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
487	shape and event stream.
488	
489	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
490	segment:
491	
492	```json
493	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
494	```
495	
496	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
497	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
498	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
499	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
500	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
501	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
502	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
503	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
504	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
505	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
506	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
507	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
508	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
509	loop node instead).
510	
511	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
512	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
513	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
514	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
515	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
516	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
517	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
518	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
519	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
520	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
521	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
522	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
523	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
524	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
525	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
526	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
527	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
528	belong only to their iterations.
529	
530	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
531	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
532	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
533	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
534	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
535	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
536	exactly.
537	
538	### Dynamic map nodes
539	
540	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
541	recorded array:
542	
543	```json
544	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
545	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
546	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
547	```
548	
549	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
550	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
551	
552	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
553	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
554	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
555	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
556	  the same path syntax as a condition.
557	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
558	  expand.
559	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
560	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
561	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
562	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
563	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
564	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
565	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
566	
567	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
568	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
569	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
570	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
571	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
572	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
573	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
574	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
575	overwrite another instance.
576	
577	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
578	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
579	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
580	become available in the usual way.
581	
582	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
583	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
584	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
585	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
586	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
587	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
588	
589	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
590	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per instance
591	giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or `failed`),
592	its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a permanently failed
593	instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and the node's single
594	`failure_reason`. The `maps` field is present only when the bound workflow
595	declares a map node outside any loop body; every other execution keeps its
596	previous state shape.
597	
598	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
599	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
600	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
601	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
602	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
603	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
604	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
605	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
606	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
607	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
608	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
609	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
610	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
611	other node event.
612	
613	### Maps inside loop bodies
614	
615	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
616	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
617	other body member:
618	
619	```json
620	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
621	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
622	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
623	```
624	
625	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
626	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
627	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
628	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
629	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
630	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
631	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
632	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
633	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
634	
635	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
636	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
637	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
638	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
639	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
640	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
641	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
642	influence from the iteration number.
643	
644	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
645	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
646	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
647	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
648	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
649	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
650	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
651	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
652	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
653	
654	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
655	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
656	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
657	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
658	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
659	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
660	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
661	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
662	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
663	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
664	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
665	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
666	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
667	
668	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
669	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
670	
671	### Workflow versions
672	
673	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
674	
675	```json
676	{
677	  "id": "order-flow",
678	  "version": "2026-09-25",
679	  "nodes": [
680	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
681	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
682	  ]
683	}
684	```
685	
686	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
687	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
688	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
689	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
690	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
691	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
692	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
693	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
694	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
695	
696	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
697	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
698	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
699	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
700	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
701	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
702	
703	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
704	current version at the moment it starts:
705	
706	```http
707	POST /executions
708	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
709	
710	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
711	```
712	
713	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
714	
715	```json
716	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
717	```
718	
719	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
720	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
721	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
722	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
723	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
724	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
725	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
726	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
727	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
728	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
729	conclusions never change.
730	
731	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
732	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
733	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
734	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
735	stream with no added field.
736	
737	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
738	
739	```http
740	GET /workflows/order-flow
741	```
742	
743	```json
744	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
745	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
746	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
747	]}
748	```
749	
750	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
751	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
752	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
753	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
754	resources as usual.
755	
756	### Migrate a running execution to another version
757	
758	```http
759	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
760	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
761	
762	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
763	```
764	
765	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
766	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
767	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
768	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
769	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
770	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
771	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
772	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
773	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
774	carries the target version.
775	
776	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
777	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
778	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
779	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
780	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
781	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
782	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
783	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
784	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
785	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
786	
787	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
788	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
789	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
790	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
791	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
792	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
793	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
794	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
795	content.
796	
797	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
798	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
799	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
800	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
801	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
802	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
803	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
804	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
805	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
806	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
807	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
808	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
809	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
810	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
811	
812	### Start an execution
813	
814	```http
815	POST /executions
816	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
817	
818	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
819	```
820	
821	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
822	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
823	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
824	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
825	
826	An execution may declare a timeout:
827	
828	```json
829	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
830	```
831	
832	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
833	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
834	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
835	a timeout never expire.
836	
837	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
838	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
839	
840	```json
841	{
842	  "id": "run-3",
843	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
844	  "input": {},
845	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
846	}
847	```
848	
849	### Inspect an execution
850	
851	```http
852	GET /executions/run-1
853	GET /executions/run-1/events
854	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
855	```
856	
857	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
858	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
859	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
860	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
861	
862	### Webhook notifications
863	
864	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
865	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
866	
867	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
868	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
869	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
870	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
871	  reason);
872	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
873	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
874	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
875	
876	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
877	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
878	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
879	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
880	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
881	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
882	subscriptions" below.
883	
884	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
885	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
886	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
887	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
888	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
889	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
890	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
891	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
892	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
893	triggered it.
894	
895	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
896	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
897	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
898	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
899	results as before.
900	
901	### Inspect the delivery history
902	
903	```http
904	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
905	```
906	
907	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
908	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
909	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
910	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
911	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
912	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
913	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
914	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
915	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
916	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
917	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
918	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
919	
920	### Queue subscriptions
921	
922	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
923	
924	```json
925	{
926	  "id": "run-4",
927	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
928	  "input": {},
929	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
930	}
931	```
932	
933	A queue subscription contains exactly:
934	
935	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
936	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
937	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
938	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
939	
940	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
941	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
942	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
943	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
944	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
945	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
946	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
947	
948	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
949	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
950	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
951	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
952	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
953	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
954	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
955	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
956	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
957	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
958	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
959	before.
960	
961	### Inspect the queue state
962	
963	```http
964	GET /executions/run-4/queues
965	X-Tenant-Id: acme
966	```
967	
968	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
969	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
970	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
971	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
972	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
973	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
974	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
975	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
976	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
977	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
978	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
979	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
980	
981	### Pull messages from a queue
982	
983	```http
984	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
985	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
986	X-Tenant-Id: acme
987	
988	{}
989	```
990	
991	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
992	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
993	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
994	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
995	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
996	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
997	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
998	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
999	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1000	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1001	
1002	### Acknowledge a message
1003	
1004	```http
1005	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1006	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
1007	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1008	
1009	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
1010	```
1011	
1012	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
1013	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
1014	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
1015	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
1016	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
1017	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
1018	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
1019	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
1020	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
1021	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
1022	`conflict`.
1023	
1024	### Schedules
1025	
1026	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
1027	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
1028	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
1029	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
1030	
1031	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
1032	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
1033	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
1034	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
1035	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
1036	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
1037	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
1038	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
1039	
1040	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
1041	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
1042	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
1043	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
1044	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
1045	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
1046	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
1047	created is exposed through the status query below.
1048	
1049	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
1050	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
1051	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
1052	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
1053	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
1054	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
1055	
1056	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
1057	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
1058	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
1059	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
1060	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
1061	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1062	
1063	### Declare or replace a schedule
1064	
1065	```http
1066	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1067	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
1068	
1069	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
1070	```
1071	
1072	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
1073	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
1074	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
1075	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
1076	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
1077	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
1078	
1079	### Inspect the schedule status
1080	
1081	```http
1082	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1083	```
1084	
1085	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
1086	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
1087	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
1088	
1089	```json
1090	{
1091	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1092	  "paused": false,
1093	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
1094	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
1095	}
1096	```
1097	
1098	The fields are:
1099	
1100	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
1101	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
1102	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
1103	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
1104	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
1105	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
1106	  `null` until the first period fires;
1107	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
1108	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
1109	
1110	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
1111	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
1112	
1113	### Pause and resume a schedule
1114	
1115	```http
1116	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
1117	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
1118	
1119	{}
1120	```
1121	
1122	```http
1123	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
1124	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
1125	
1126	{}
1127	```
1128	
1129	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
1130	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
1131	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
1132	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
1133	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
1134	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
1135	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1136	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1137	
1138	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1139	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1140	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
1141	
1142	### Checkpoints
1143	
1144	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
1145	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
1146	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
1147	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
1148	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
1149	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
1150	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
1151	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
1152	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
1153	duplicating any node output.
1154	
1155	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
1156	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
1157	same state shape and event stream as before.
1158	
1159	### Complete the next ready node
1160	
1161	```http
1162	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1163	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
1164	
1165	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
1166	```
1167	
1168	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
1169	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
1170	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
1171	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
1172	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
1173	the status becomes `completed`.
1174	
1175	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
1176	
1177	```http
1178	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1179	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
1180	
1181	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
1182	```
1183	
1184	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
1185	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
1186	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
1187	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
1188	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
1189	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
1190	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
1191	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
1192	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
1193	
1194	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
1195	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
1196	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
1197	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
1198	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
1199	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
1200	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
1201	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
1202	the execution stream.
1203	
1204	### Cancel an execution
1205	
1206	```http
1207	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
1208	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
1209	```
1210	
1211	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
1212	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
1213	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
1214	
1215	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
1216	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
1217	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
1218	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
1219	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
1220	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
1221	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
1222	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
1223	
1224	### Claim a work item
1225	
1226	```http
1227	POST /executions/run-1/claim
1228	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
1229	
1230	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
1231	```
1232	
1233	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
1234	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
1235	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
1236	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
1237	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
1238	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
1239	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
1240	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
1241	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
1242	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
1243	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
1244	
1245	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
1246	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
1247	
1248	```http
1249	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1250	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
1251	
1252	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1253	```
1254	
1255	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
1256	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
1257	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
1258	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
1259	an execution without any claim.
1260	
1261	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
1262	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
1263	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
1264	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
1265	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
1266	
1267	### Renew a lease
1268	
1269	```http
1270	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
1271	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
1272	
1273	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1274	```
1275	
1276	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
1277	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
1278	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
1279	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
1280	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
1281	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
1282	
1283	### Release a work item
1284	
1285	```http
1286	POST /executions/run-1/release
1287	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
1288	
1289	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1290	```
1291	
1292	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
1293	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
1294	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
1295	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
1296	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
1297	`not_found`.
1298	
1299	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
1300	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
1301	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
1302	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
1303	restarts.
1304	
1305	### Recover from a checkpoint
1306	
1307	```http
1308	POST /executions/run-1/recover
1309	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
1310	
1311	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
1312	```
1313	
1314	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
1315	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
1316	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
1317	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
1318	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
1319	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
1320	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
1321	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
1322	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
1323	execution state and events.
1324	
1325	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
1326	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
1327	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
1328	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
1329	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
1330	stays consistent with the materialized state.
1331	
1332	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
1333	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
1334	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
1335	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
1336	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
1337	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
1338	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
1339	
1340	### Replay
1341	
1342	```http
1343	POST /executions/run-1/replay
1344	```
1345	
1346	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
1347	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
1348	and the rebuilt execution.
1349	
1350	## Errors
1351	
1352	Errors use this shape:
1353	
1354	```json
1355	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
1356	```
1357	
1358	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
1359	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
1360	declarations and the usage, bill, and metrics queries require a tenant, and
1361	quota limits are positive integers validated by the
1362	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
1363	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
1364	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
1365	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
1366	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1367	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1368	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1369	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1370	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1371	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1372	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1373	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1374	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1375	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1376	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1377	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1378	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1379	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1380	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1381	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, more than ten attempts, a
1382	subscription declaring both `url` and `queue` or neither, an empty queue
1383	name, or a non-positive visibility timeout — is a
1384	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1385	querying the delivery history or the queues of a missing execution is a
1386	missing resource. Declaring a queue name another workflow or execution of
1387	the same tenant already declared is a conflict. Pulling from or
1388	acknowledging a missing queue, and acknowledging an unknown or already
1389	acknowledged message, are missing resources; a pull body that is not an
1390	empty object, or an acknowledgement body without exactly an
1391	`idempotency_key` string, is a validation error. An approval
1392	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1393	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1394	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1395	A map node with an unknown or missing field, a mistyped or non-positive
1396	`max_instances`, an invalid template, a `source` that is not a
1397	task dependency, or an invalid `path` is likewise a validation error that
1398	rejects the whole request, whether the map stands alone or sits inside a
1399	loop body.
1400	A decision by an approver who is
1401	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1402	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1403	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1404	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1405	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1406	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1407	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1408	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1409	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1410	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1411	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1412	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1413	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1414	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1415	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1416	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1417	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1418	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1419	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1420	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
